words.g: f. loc. pl.; compound (see Samāsa); locative of the goal, with कणमोक्ष- in 1.52

sandhi.note: The m of तुल्यम् joins the vowel; t stays t before t; ā + u → o (तथोभयोः).
Final e before a: the a is absorbed (avagraha).

Final n before ś becomes the palatal ñ, and the ś becomes ch. In the full derivation a t is optionally inserted after the n, made palatal, and then lost; the Gita Press writes the result ञ्छ (compare the variant note on 3.22). Without the change the words would be written पतङ्गान् शाव-.

samasa.literal: in the beaks of the young

morph.note: Locative of the present participle of √अस् ‘to be’: ज्ञाने सति ‘knowledge being (present)’, a locative absolute; with अपि it is concessive: ‘even though they have knowledge’.
√दृश् has no present of its own; the stem पश्य- serves for the present system. Imperative 2nd sg.: ‘look!’
Neuter nominative of the pronominal adjective अन्य, with -त् as in तत्, यत्: ‘the other (things)’.

mantras.anvaya: मनुष्याणां च यत् (ज्ञानम्), (तत्) तेषाम् (अपि अस्ति); अन्यत् (च) तथा उभयोः तुल्यम्। ज्ञाने सति अपि, एतान् पतङ्गान् पश्य, शावचञ्चुषु (कणमोक्षादृतान् …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line: a relative clause with its correlative understood, then a nominal clause. The second line: a concessive locative absolute and the imperative पश्य with its object पतङ्गान्, described further in 1.52.
mantras.lit: And what is men’s is theirs; and the rest is likewise equal for both. Even though there is knowledge, look at these birds — into the beaks of their young
mantras.tr: and what men have, they have; in all else, too, the two are alike. Yet, for all their knowledge, look at these birds — into the beaks of their young
mantras.tr_note: The sentence runs on into 1.52: the birds are intent on dropping grain into those beaks.

comm.t: Medhas closes the comparison (humans and animals are alike in knowledge and in the rest) and points to an example. The demonstrative एतान् with the imperative पश्य suggests birds within sight at the hermitage.
The text does not say what ‘the rest’ (अन्यत्) is; the point is only that, in the ordinary life of the senses, humans and animals are on one level.

samasa.type: saptamī tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (कणमोक्ष)
samasa.literal: devoted to the release of grains
samasa.sense: intent on dropping food into their young’s beaks

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (upamita: the standard of comparison stands second)
samasa.sense: a heroic address to the king
samasa.alt: Also resolved as a saptamī tatpuruṣa, मनुजेषु व्याघ्रः ‘a tiger among men’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Passive present participle: passive stem पीड्य- (yak) + -मान. ‘Being tormented’, with the agent क्षुधा in the instrumental.
Ablative of cause: the birds act ‘from delusion’, not from calculation — the contrast with लोभात् (‘from greed’) in 1.53.
As a postposition (karmapravacanīya) प्रति takes the accusative: सुतान् प्रति ‘toward (their) sons’.

mantras.anvaya: (पतङ्गान्) मोहात् कणमोक्षादृतान्, क्षुधा पीड्यमानान् अपि (पश्य)। (हे) मनुजव्याघ्र, मानुषाः सुतान् प्रति साभिलाषाः (भवन्ति), …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the description of the birds (objects of पश्य in 1.51). The second begins a new statement about humans; its cause comes in 1.53.
mantras.lit: — intent, out of delusion, on letting fall grains, though tormented by hunger. Human beings, O tiger among men, are full of longing toward their sons
mantras.tr: they drop grain into them out of sheer delusion, though racked by hunger themselves. Men, tiger among men, long for sons
mantras.tr_note: ‘themselves’ makes plain that the hunger is the parent birds’ own. The second line runs on into 1.53.

comm.t: The birds feed their young while starving themselves, and the sage calls the motive मोह, delusion. Then he turns to humans, who also long for their children.

The two cases are not the same: the birds act from blind delusion, humans (1.53) from greed for a return. Both are forms of the attachment the king asked about, and both, Medhas says next, are the work of Mahāmāyā (1.54).

sandhi.note: The final t stays unvoiced before p; the words are only written together. Inside प्रत्युपकार, प्रति + उप- gives प्रत्युप- (इको यणचि, 6.1.77).
Final u before e becomes v.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (a metaphor, rūpaka: the first member is identified with the second)
samasa.literal: in the whirlpool that is mine-ness
samasa.sense: caught in the circling pull of possessiveness
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, ममतायाः आवर्त्तः ‘the whirlpool of mine-ness’; the metaphorical reading fits the paired image मोहगर्ते.

samasa.literal: in the pit that is delusion
samasa.sense: fallen into bewilderment as into a pit
samasa.alt: Also ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, मोहस्य गर्तः; as above.

morph.note: Past passive participle of the causative of नि + √पत्: ‘made to fall, thrown down’. The causer is named in the next verse: by the power of Mahāmāyā (1.54).

ममता (मम + -ता) is the same idea as ममत्व in 1.41 and 1.44. आवर्त्त ‘whirlpool’ (आ + √वृत् ‘to turn’) is printed with a doubled t after r, a spelling the grammarians permit; it is the same word as आवर्त.
प्रत्युपकार ‘a service in return’ (प्रति + उपकार); the dative gives the purpose: parents cherish children ‘for the sake of a return’.

mantras.anvaya: (मानुषाः) लोभात् प्रत्युपकाराय (सुतान् प्रति साभिलाषाः)। ननु एतान् किं न पश्यसि? तथा अपि (एते) ममतावर्त्ते मोहगर्ते निपातिताः (महामायाप्रभावेण, 1.54)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first half finishes 1.52 (why men long for sons) and asks a rhetorical question. The second begins the sentence completed in 1.54: the beings are thrown into mamatā and moha by the power of Mahāmāyā.
mantras.lit: — out of greed, for a return of the favour. Surely you see these? Even so, (they are) cast down into the whirlpool of mine-ness, into the pit of delusion,
mantras.tr: out of greed, hoping to be repaid. Do you not see them? And still they are thrown into the whirlpool of ‘mine’, into the pit of delusion —
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is completed in 1.54: ‘by the power of Mahāmāyā, who keeps the world of saṃsāra in being’.

comm.t: Human love for children is mixed with self-interest: greed for a return. Yet humans and birds alike, knowing as they are, are thrown into the same whirlpool of possessiveness and pit of delusion. The next verse names who throws them.

The two images answer the king’s words: his ममत्व (1.41, 1.44) and मोह (1.44) return as the whirlpool and the pit. The sage’s answer is that this is not a private failure of the king and the merchant but the working of Mahāmāyā (1.54–56), who is also the cause of release (1.57).

The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess from the other side of the same pair: ममताहन्त्री (165), ‘destroyer of mine-ness’, and मोहनाशिनी (163), ‘remover of delusion’. Here in the Devī Māhātmya the same power that casts beings into mamatā and moha is the one that frees them when she is gracious (1.57).
